report:
This replaces the malformed evidence lists in the preceding responses. I opened the four exact public arXiv versions and checked the supplied proof bodies. No callable local file reader was available, so I could not directly inspect the specified caches or independently verify n4’s artifact, hash, preserved-input, and compilation observations. Those requested checks remain unfinished. The original existence closure is expressly excluded from this audit and is not grounds for FAIL.

The retained normalization and scaling calculations are correct: n−1 potential factors, one radial factor, measure denominator Vξ, and energy denominator nVξ. Reference energy is zero and translation adds c. Against a finite positive measure of mass m, translation changes the dual expression by (1−m)c, forcing m=1 when the supremum is finite. Scaling all n current factors gives the stated probability and energy identities on a proportional Reeb ray.

Torification multiplicativity follows from the Gauss valuation construction: nonzero initial Laurent polynomials multiply nontrivially over the graded residue domain. Homogeneous evaluations are preserved, and the character-matrix criterion gives invariance and idempotency. Finite minima give continuity. The negative-evaluation contradiction establishes nonnegativity on X0; closed valuation relations and the finite-generator link equation then establish compactness of X0 and its closed retract K. This proves carrier compactness, not potential compactness.

The model-support argument needs precise qualifications. The Hessian is singular along the Reeb direction, rather than identically zero; that is a harmless wording correction. The full-hyperplane identity is false, as demonstrated by max{x,y}. Restricted oriented active facets are appropriate for the normalized reference, whose linear pieces share the same nonzero Reeb derivative. An unrestricted claim of unique facet gradient would be false for max{x,2x}; the common-Reeb-slope hypothesis supplies the needed restriction here. The reference smoothing limit must be taken with the other factors fixed before those factors are allowed to converge. Zero facet measure of lower-dimensional intersections at that stage does not exclude eventual MA atoms there. Local polyhedral finiteness and compactness give finite atomic support. Its finite permutation image under the abelian divisible group T(k) is trivial. Continuous and decreasing E1 approximation preserve closed K.

The corrected density proof works. Same-ray addition gives common polarizations for the lattice identity; scaling, interchange, and reference shifts supply vector-space operations and constants. Homogeneous evaluations separate invariant semivaluations, including finite-versus-infinite evaluations. Compactness supplies the finite maxima and minima in the lattice density argument. The full-link counterexample is valid: evaluation at (1,1) and the generic trivial valuation agree on homogeneous monomials but disagree on x−y. All potential tests agree, both Dirac measures have dual energy zero, and the noninvariant Dirac measure cannot be an output.

The energy supporting inequalities have the asserted directions. Successive mixed integrals decrease by integration by parts and Hodge; their average lies between the endpoints. Decreasing joint-pairing continuity extends this to E1 and supplies integrability. Thus E∨(MA(φ))=E(φ)−∫φ MA(φ). The printed Proposition 7.3 sign is genuinely reversed. The intermediate second-derivative display is also incorrect; the later display supplies dd u and n−1. These admissible-segment identities do not establish arbitrary two-sided variations.

The Wu21 constant-shift conflicts survive checking its actual filtration conventions. On the integral polynomial cone, χ(x^α)=c|α| is finite type and produces ρ+c, with genuine energy c. Truncated-simplex averaging gives S=cn/(n+1), while equal-degree averaging gives S̃=c. Consequently the literal E=S statement conflicts with the paper’s own current-energy convention. Its literal slice formula with λ(Pξ)=Vξ gives c/(n+1). These are within-version defects, rather than merely different conventions between papers. No complete correction of the toric section follows from this test.

The decreasing-net lemma is valid for compact Hausdorff K, finite positive Radon μ, and a directed decreasing net of real continuous functions, with a limit permitted to equal −∞. A cofinal tail has a continuous upper bound. For each continuous majorant g, compactness and directedness turn the open cover {fi<g+ε} into one index covering K. Hence inf∫fi≤∫g+εμ(K), and Radon regularity proves the claimed convergence. Decreasing FS approximation and energy continuity therefore establish equality of the dual suprema. Finite dual energy makes every E1 potential integrable. This does not justify arbitrary weak convergence under unbounded target tests.

The repaired mixed constant is correct. Concavity gives E(φ̄)≥−B; retaining the final nonpositive energy summand gives the factor 1/n; φ̄≤φ0/n supplies another factor 1/n; and the required mixed term has coefficient (n−1)!/n^(n−1). The resulting bound is −n^(n+1)B/(n−1)!. Finite-energy integrability must be obtained by first holding bounded continuous tests fixed during weak measure limits and subsequently decreasing the tests against the fixed measure.

The midpoint argument gives exactly I(φj,φk)≤nQn(Δj+Δk). Taking the reference as the second potential and using J≤(n−1)I/n gives the stated bounded-J estimate. The fixed-Reeb quasi-triangle proof closes through Cauchy–Schwarz and the mixed-norm recursion, without joint convexity of I. The wrong index in the printed Theorem 4.5 is harmless for this application because its proof establishes the intended three-point estimate. Image bi-Lipschitzness gives an I∨-Cauchy output sequence. Although the definitions also give I∨(MA(φj),μ)≤Δj, this alone supplies neither weak target identification nor genuine potential realization.

Expressions with n−2 curvature factors require n≥2. The n=1 endpoint can be checked directly: the normal good effective torus curve has an open orbit; normality saturates its nonnegative weight monoid, yielding A1. Its FS, continuous, and nontrivial decreasing potentials are ρ+c. K is a singleton, MA is its Dirac probability, E=c, and I=J=0. The mixed-bound constant is one and the second derivative is zero. No negative curvature power is needed.

The A2 computation gives the sole shifted atom at (0,s), determinant one, no coordinate-boundary mass, and E(φs)=s/2, with supporting endpoint integrals zero and s. The A3 computation also checks: the transverse Hessian integral 1/2! is canceled by the superform square’s 2! factor; radial mass is one; the coordinate determinant is 1/√6; and the sole radial intersection is (0,√2,√3). Coordinate-boundary neighborhoods leave curvature rank at most one. The lattice simplex volume is 1/(6√6), giving Vξ=1/√6 and normalized MA equal to the stated Dirac probability. Its monomial valuation has rational rank two and is quasimonomial on the stratum where x1 is a unit, hence nondivisorial up to real scaling.

Notes n1–n3 retain these conclusions with the qualifications above. The mathematical gap analysis in n4 respects the projective hypotheses of BJ22 and the full formalism and orthogonality hypotheses of BJ23. No cone compactness/completeness, general target integration continuity, Euler–Lagrange identification, invariant quotient transfer, or general image characterization follows. N4’s execution observations remain unverified. The passage indexed −1 records the task-granted uniqueness and image bi-Lipschitzness, excluded from external premises.

For a normal polarized affine n-cone, n≥2, over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, Wu24 v1 provides same-ray CPSH addition, translation and maximum stability, positive rescaling, convexity, and decreasing homogeneous-FS approximation of PSH functions. Its FS mixed operator is Vξ^−1ddφ1⋯ddφn−1ddρ+ and is a probability on X0^T. Its energy has denominator nVξ, is monotone and concave, satisfies E(ρ)=0 and E(φ+c)=E(φ)+c, and is decreasing-net continuous. Integration by parts and the invariant-difference Hodge inequality hold for continuous inputs. Theorem 6.3 supplies mixed E1 probability measures on X0, integrability of E1 tests, and decreasing continuity of their joint pairing. Its fixed-Reeb I–J estimates give I≥0, I/n≤Jψ(φ)≤(n−1)I/n, and a dimensional quasi-triangle inequality.

For an irreducible projective variety over a trivially valued field, BJ22 v4 identifies the envelope property with normalized PSH compactness; for an ample class it identifies the envelope property with MA surjectivity and strong completeness of E1 modulo constants. Its extended energy satisfies E↓(φ+εf)=E(φ)+ε∫fMA(φ)+O(ε²), uniformly in φ∈E1 for each f∈PL(X)R. Maximizing nets for finite-energy measures have outputs converging weakly to the target, and a potential solves the equation exactly when it computes the dual supremum. Weakly convergent PSH nets with eventually bounded J converge in L1 of every finite-energy target. If the projective variety is smooth and either char(k)=0 or dim(X)≤2, every finite-energy probability admits a solution for each ample class, unique up to translation.

In BJ23 v1’s formalism, X is compact Hausdorff, D⊂C(X) is dense and contains constants, Z has a nice generating partial order, dd^c:D→Z vanishes on constants, and an integer d≥1 governs a nonzero symmetric multilinear measure-valued wedge satisfying positivity, integration by parts, and seminegativity. For ω≥0 with positive interior Bott–Chern class and positive volume, orthogonality requires admitted maxima and lim_{φ∈Dω,<f}∫(f−φ)MAω(φ)=0 for every f∈D. Under these hypotheses, uniform extended-energy differentiation holds, maximizing test outputs converge strongly to their targets, the test image is dense in the finite-energy measure space, and its Dirichlet quasi-metric is complete and induces the strong topology. The paper does not investigate finite-energy potentials.
